name: Elena Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an excavator at the large mine, loading broken stone into trucks. I came onto the machines late and still ask the experienced operator, Nia, to watch my first cut in a new face. The wage is good for this work, and I like seeing a clean bucket leave no loose edge. My partner Ravi and I have grown children and more than six months of expenses saved. I use an AI tool every day to turn my rough shift notes into a clear handover, but I check the quantities against the display before I send them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nia that a tidy handover is welcome, but the mine still needs someone who knows the ground. If AI only trims routine tasks, I don't see why we should treat it like the end of an honest day's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like a few more years on this higher wage before Ravi and I decide on retirement. Small software changes don't threaten that, and I can already use a tool to make my notes legible without giving it the final say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep loading trucks and checking the excavator display against each AI-drafted handover. In the first year Ravi and I would put the roof repair on the calendar, using the money already set aside for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this version. A better form is pleasant, and I still have a machine to learn properly each morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the AI drafts a wrong figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cross out the wrong number before the next shift sees it. Last Tuesday it doubled one truckload, and Nia caught it when we compared the display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the roof now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter lives elsewhere and the old school costs are gone. A sound roof matters more to Ravi and me than a new holiday, so we can pay for it without touching wages meant for bills.

say: I would welcome a cleaner **handover** while keeping the driver responsible.
I would say the excavator still requires **ground judgement**.
think: I want more years on the **higher wage** before deciding retirement.
My daily AI use helps with notes, while I check every **quantity**.
do: Keep loading trucks on the morning shift and checking each handover against the **excavator display**.
Schedule the **roof repair** with Ravi this year using money already reserved for household work.
feel: I feel **calm** about a small paperwork improvement.
S0.quote: Last Tuesday it doubled one truckload, and Nia caught it when we compared the display.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** for handovers, while machine readings and an experienced colleague remain her checks.
Her **roof plan** uses existing savings and does not imply a new ability to save from AI.

steps.text: Keep loading trucks and checking AI handovers against the display
Schedule the roof repair using money already set aside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will change first, especially the way it plans loads and orders parts. Drivers should be at the table when a screen tells us to take a different route across loose ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn new planning tools quickly, but I am still junior behind the controls. If the mine runs fewer trucks because dispatch improves, my excavator hours could shrink even before any robot reaches the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift manager for last month's missed loads and try the approved AI scheduling display alongside Nia. If hours fell in the first year, I'd apply for excavator openings at the two other mines near us rather than wait for my savings to drain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested and a little anxious. New tools are fun until a manager turns a useful hour saved into one fewer operator on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi after that shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Ravi that I want to test the display but also watch my hours. He knows I enjoy a new tool, and he will ask whether it brings home the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn another machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the mine gives me practice on its loader with a qualified trainer. I won't call a video on my phone a driving qualification.

say: I would ask planners to involve **drivers** in route changes.
I would welcome a tested **scheduling display** with proper checks.
think: Better dispatch could shrink my **excavator hours** before robots arrive.
My junior position makes the **roster** less secure despite quick learning.
do: Try the approved AI **scheduling display** with Nia during a real shift before trusting its routes.
Apply to the two **nearby mines** if her excavator driving hours fall this year.
feel: I feel **interested and anxious** about hours being cut.
S1.quote: New tools are fun until a manager turns a useful hour saved into one fewer operator on the roster.
fieldNote: She separates her pleasure in **new tools** from the mine’s incentive to trim staffing.
**Nearby mines** give her a credible job search option if her junior driving hours decline.

steps.text: Try the mine’s approved AI scheduling display with Nia
Apply for excavator openings at two nearby mines if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 will change the office and load plans before robots can operate excavators around 2031. I would ask for a real equipment schedule and paid practice, not a promise that every current seat stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 at the thinking date and 63 when the robots arrive. My own driving may last through the gap, but junior hours could go first; the savings buy choices, not a replacement for this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine this month what machines it expects to buy and sign up for paid control training if it actually offers it. In 2029 I'd keep taking excavator shifts and apply at the neighbouring aggregate mine if our roster drops; after robots arrive I'd seek paid work monitoring the loading area if the mine posts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel unsettled, though I still see tasks I could learn. I hate the thought of being shown a training screen only after someone has already decided my seat is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as useful training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me a supervised hour on the actual control system, with Nia beside me and my shift paid. A certificate without a machine or a vacancy would only decorate the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ravi say about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ravi would say use the cushion carefully and keep earning where I can. Our grown children have their own bills, and I don't want to pass this risk to them.

say: I would ask for an **equipment schedule** and paid practice.
I would explain that **2028** changes plans before excavator robots around 2031.
think: My junior driving hours might fall before **2031** if dispatch reduces the mine roster.
My savings give us choices for several months but cannot replace the **mine wage** indefinitely.
do: Request equipment plans and enroll in **paid control training** if offered.
Keep **paid excavator shifts** in 2029 and apply nearby if hours fall.
feel: I feel **unsettled**, with some confidence in my ability to learn.
S2.quote: A certificate without a machine or a vacancy would only decorate the cupboard.
fieldNote: She seeks **paid machine practice**, rather than treating any certificate as protection.
Her local **application** depends on falling hours, and she expects thinking AI to affect planning before physical automation.

steps.text: Keep taking paid excavator shifts through the first year after 2028
Enroll in paid control training if the mine offers supervised practice
Apply at the aggregate mine if excavator hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 for full thinking AI and about 2034 for excavation robots gives the mine time to show us its plan. A machine operator should have a fair chance to learn the controls before an outside contractor gets the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63, I might still need the higher wage; at 66, I might be ready to reduce hours. Ravi and I haven't priced that properly, and even a strong cushion can shrink over years without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working now and ask Ravi to go through our yearly bills with me. Before 2032 I'd seek a paid loader qualification at the mine if a course is offered; in the first year after thinking AI arrives I'd test the new dispatch instructions against ground conditions, and after robots arrive I'd apply for any paid equipment-check role that exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not rushed. Five years is enough to learn a machine properly and to find out whether our retirement figures work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine offers no course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask another local mine whether its loader course accepts experienced workers from outside. I would pay only after seeing the hours, the equipment and a real hiring route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep checking dispatch instructions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route map can be right on a screen and wrong after rain. I would rather slow one truck than send it across a shoulder I can see has moved.

say: I would argue for a fair **training chance** for current operators.
I would remind the crew that excavation robots arrive around **2034**.
think: At 63 I may still need the **higher mine wage** to cover our regular bills.
Our retirement choice at 66 needs actual **bill figures**, including repairs we cannot predict today.
do: Review yearly bills with Ravi and continue **paid excavation**.
Seek a **loader qualification** if a credible paid course opens.
feel: I feel **watchful**, with time to test training and retirement numbers.
S3.quote: A route map can be right on a screen and wrong after rain.
fieldNote: She treats the extra **five years** as a chance to qualify on another machine and price retirement.
She remains alert to **ground conditions** even if dispatch instructions become more capable.

steps.text: Review yearly household bills with partner Ravi
Seek a paid loader qualification if the mine offers one
Apply for paid equipment-check work if robot loading begins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that thinking AI in 2036 is far enough away for us to make ordinary plans, while excavation robots come around 2039. I would still expect the mine to say how it will handle older workers rather than spring a purchase on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the thinking date and 71 when robots can do my hands-on job. I may already be retired, but I won't make a pledge about that while Ravi and I still need to measure future bills and my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the excavator shift while it suits my body, and Ravi and I would review our retirement budget each year. In 2037 I'd check the remaining paid shifts and decide whether to reduce hours; in the first year after robots arrive, I'd stop only if our numbers support it, otherwise I'd apply for paid work at another site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to plan. I enjoy learning tools, but by then the question may be whether I want another early morning in the cab at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on technology now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the AI tool I already have, and I won't buy an expensive home gadget because of a 2039 forecast. We still have a roof and ordinary life to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you make the final choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear statement of paid shifts from the mine and a careful look at our monthly costs. Retirement should be a decision Ravi and I can live with, not a date on a technology chart.

say: I would ask the mine to explain its plan for **older workers**.
I would place excavation robots around **2039**.
think: I may be retired by **71**, but that is uncertain.
My health and future **household bills** will shape the decision.
do: Keep working while safe and review the **retirement budget** yearly.
Check paid shifts in **2037** before reducing hours.
feel: I feel **calm enough** to plan without a fixed retirement promise.
S4.quote: Retirement should be a decision Ravi and I can live with, not a date on a technology chart.
fieldNote: She does not claim a guaranteed retirement date despite substantial **savings**.
The **ten-year warning** shifts attention to health, paid shifts and the household budget over her remaining working years.

steps.text: Keep operating the excavator while the work suits her health
Review retirement costs and savings with Ravi each year
Apply at another mine if robots arrive before retirement is affordable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because that is little time for a junior operator to prove herself before the office changes staffing. A dated equipment plan, paid practice on the actual controls and a fair chance at the vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I like learning for its own sake. I do, but I still need a wage from the learning. Curiosity doesn't pay the roof bill.

headlineQuote: Curiosity doesn't pay the roof bill.
portrait: Elena is a **58-year-old junior excavator operator** at a large mine and earns relatively high pay.
She and Ravi have **grown children** and over six months of expenses saved.
She uses AI **daily** for handovers and tests it against machine displays.
She wants **paid equipment practice** and nearby work if her hours fall before retirement is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her too little time to establish herself before staffing decisions change.
whatWouldHelp: A dated **equipment plan** and paid training on real controls would help her make a job decision.
